flashcards.a: Under an actual network partition, a distributed system must choose between Consistency (linearizability) and Availability (every non-failing node responds) -- cannot guarantee both plus Partition tolerance simultaneously during a partition.

flashcards.q: What's wrong with "CAP means pick two of three"?
flashcards.a: Partition tolerance isn't optional in a real multi-node system (partitions will happen), so the only live choice is CP vs AP, and only DURING an actual partition. Outside a partition, a system can be fully consistent and fully available simultaneously.

flashcards.q: How does CAP's "Availability" differ from a 99.99% uptime SLA?
flashcards.a: CAP's A is binary and instantaneous per-request: every request to a non-failing node gets SOME non-error response, with no statement about latency. An SLA is a statistical, time-averaged measure that typically implies a latency bound too.

flashcards.q: How does CAP's "C" differ from ACID's "C"?
flashcards.a: ACID consistency = transactions preserve application-defined invariants (foreign keys, uniqueness). CAP consistency = all nodes agree on the current value of a piece of data (linearizability). Same letter, unrelated concepts.

flashcards.q: State PACELC and explain why it's more useful than CAP alone.
flashcards.a: If Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency. More useful because real systems spend ~99.99% of time in the 'Else' branch, which CAP is entirely silent about.

flashcards.q: Classify Spanner and DynamoDB/Cassandra in PACELC terms.
flashcards.a: Spanner = PC/EC (always consistent, pays latency cost via TrueTime commit-wait even with no partition). Dynamo/Cassandra = PA/EL by default (available and fast; consistency is a tunable knob usually loosened).

flashcards.q: Rank linearizable, sequential, causal, eventual consistency and state what each permits.
flashcards.a: Linearizable: real-time total order, as if one copy. Sequential: one shared total order respecting each process's own order, but not tied to real time across processes. Causal: only causally-related ops ordered; concurrent ops can differ across replicas. Eventual: only convergence guaranteed given no new writes, no ordering guarantee otherwise.

flashcards.q: What do read-your-writes and monotonic-reads session guarantees fix?
flashcards.a: Read-your-writes: a client sees its own prior writes (or newer) on subsequent reads even if it hits a lagging replica. Monotonic reads: successive reads by the same client never go backward in time across different replicas.

flashcards.q: State the R+W>N quorum arithmetic and what it guarantees vs doesn't.
flashcards.a: If R+W>N, every read quorum and write quorum share at least one replica, guaranteeing a read sees the most recent completed write. It does NOT guarantee real-time recency for concurrent operations -- two racing ops can still need reconciliation (vector clocks, LWW).

flashcards.q: Compare single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless replication in one line each.
flashcards.a: Single-leader: simple, no write conflicts, leader is bottleneck+SPOF, async replicas can be stale. Multi-leader: better cross-region write latency, needs conflict resolution (LWW/CRDT/app-merge). Leaderless/quorum: no single point of failure, tunable per-op consistency via R/W/N.

flashcards.q: What's the hot-partition failure mode for range partitioning, and for hash partitioning?
flashcards.a: Range: a monotonically increasing key (timestamp, auto-increment ID) concentrates all new writes on the partition owning the tail of the range. Hash: fixes that, but kills range scans (scatter-gather) and doesn't fix a single wildly popular key overloading the one partition that owns it.

flashcards.q: How does Spanner achieve external consistency, and at what latency cost?
flashcards.a: TrueTime exposes clock uncertainty as a bounded interval; the leader waits out that uncertainty (commit-wait) before acknowledging a commit, guaranteeing the timestamp has passed in real time. Measured commit-wait: ~5-8ms single-region, 20ms+ multi-region -- a permanent latency tax on every write.

flashcards.q: What consistency levels does Cassandra expose per query, and what does LOCAL_QUORUM mean?
flashcards.a: ONE, QUORUM (majority across ALL datacenters), LOCAL_QUORUM (majority within the coordinator's own datacenter only, avoiding cross-region latency), ALL. Consistency is tunable per query, not fixed at the system level.

flashcards.q: What does DynamoDB's managed service default to for read consistency, and what's the opt-in alternative?
flashcards.a: Default reads are eventually consistent (effectively R=1). An explicit option for strongly consistent reads exists, reading from the partition's current leader-equivalent copy.
